A paramour is a person's secret romantic or sexual partner — someone they are involved with outside of their marriage or committed relationship. In the simplest terms, a paramour is the person someone is having an affair with.

Think of it this way: if a married person falls in love with someone who is not their spouse, and they carry on a hidden romantic relationship with that person, that hidden partner is their paramour.
The Key Ideas Packed Into This Word

The word "paramour" is not just a fancy word for "girlfriend" or "boyfriend." It carries specific meaning. There are a few things always implied when this word is used:

1. There is an existing, official relationship being betrayed.
A paramour exists because someone is already in a marriage or a serious, committed partnership. Without that primary relationship, the word doesn't quite apply. The paramour is, by nature, the other person — the one on the side.

2. The relationship is secret or forbidden.
A paramour is not someone you bring to family dinners or introduce to friends openly. The relationship is hidden, often shameful in the eyes of society, and carried out discreetly. There is always a sense of something illicit — something that violates a promise or social expectation.

3. It implies genuine romantic or emotional depth, not just a casual encounter.
A paramour is not just a one-night stand. The word implies an ongoing connection — one that has some emotional or romantic weight to it. It is a relationship, even if a secret one.

A paramour can be any gender. A woman can be a man's paramour. A man can be a woman's paramour. Unlike the word "mistress" — which refers specifically to a woman who is the secret lover of a married man — "paramour" is completely gender-neutral, which makes it a broader and more flexible word.
What Tone Does This Word Carry?

"Paramour" is a formal and literary word. It has a slightly old-fashioned, even poetic feel to it. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Classic and modern literature (novels, poetry, plays)
  • Journalism and formal writing (especially when reporting on scandals)
  • Historical writing (it was widely used in earlier centuries)

In everyday casual conversation, people rarely say "paramour." They are more likely to say "affair partner," "secret lover," or just "the person they were seeing on the side." But when a writer or journalist does use "paramour," it immediately signals a relationship that is illicit and romantic — and it does so with elegance and precision.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are some examples to see the word in action:

  • "The king's paramour was a noblewoman from the south, whose identity was an open secret at court."
  • "When the letters were discovered, the truth about her paramour came to light."
  • "He had kept his paramour hidden from his family for three years."
  • "The scandal broke when the senator's paramour spoke to the press."

In each of these, you can feel the secrecy, the romance, and the forbidden nature of the relationship.

It helps to see how this word sits alongside related words:

  • Lover — A "lover" simply means someone you have a romantic or sexual relationship with. It does not automatically imply that anyone is cheating or that there is an existing relationship being betrayed. A paramour is always a type of lover, but not every lover is a paramour.
  • Mistress — A "mistress" refers specifically to a woman who is the secret lover of a man who is already married or committed. "Paramour" covers the same idea but applies to any gender.
  • Spouse / Partner — These are the official, public, recognized relationships. The paramour is the opposite of this — hidden, unofficial, and existing in the shadows of the official relationship.
One Sentence to Remember It By

If you ever want to recall what "paramour" means in a flash, remember this:

A paramour is the secret lover someone keeps while they are already committed to someone else.

Everything else about the word — its formality, its suggestion of ongoing romance, its gender-neutrality — flows naturally from that core idea.
